newsitem.title: PERU: Hostage crisis highlights cultural contrasts.
newsitem.headline: Hostage crisis highlights cultural contrasts.

text.p: Concern for the well-being of their loved ones unites both Peruvian and Japanese relatives of the 73 hostages being held by Marxist rebels, but the contrasting cultures have produced very different ways of showing it.

Families and friends of the approximately two dozen Japanese diplomats and businessmen being held by the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) at the Japanese ambassador's residence since Dec. 17 have concentrated on private messages of support.
"The (Japanese health ministry's) doctor said letters from families are the most effective means of communication for hostages," a diplomat of Japan's crisis task force in Peru said.

By contrast, relatives and friends of Latin American hostages have frequently shown up at the siege site to publicly express their support for their loved ones, welcoming the attention of the world media.
A group of family members and colleagues of Peru's captive deputy energy minister Jorge San Roman celebrated his 57th birthday on Friday with music and banners proclaiming "We Love You Jorge."
A Mexican mariachi version of the traditional birthday song "Las Mananitas" was followed by an improvised rendition of "Jailhouse Rock" for the ears of the music-loving minister.
San Roman's wife told local radio: "I don't know what it's like inside, but we are both hostages of this situation."

The daughter of Bolivian ambassador Jorge Gumucio, another hostage, persuaded police to let her play a cassette of Bolivian folk music over loudspeakers for her father on Jan. 10. Gumucio appeared at a window of the residence waving and smiling, witnesses said.
"Latin Americans are cheerful by nature. We are more reserved," an official of a Japanese company in Lima told Reuters.
He added that the crisis had affected friendships among Japanese wives in Peru.

Wives whose husbands were among the more than 430 hostages released so far have felt awkward about contacting friends who are still waiting for theirs to come out, even among close friends, the company official said.
Another reason Japanese relatives of the hostages tend to be more reserved is concern that too much media exposure will endanger companies and the lives of the Japanese community in Peru, he added.
Referring to local magazine "Caretas," which in its latest issue published photographs and information on all the Japanese businessmen still being held hostage, the official said:
"We are worried that somebody could use the name of the MRTA and demand ransom. We have had bomb threats by terrorists (before)."
It is not just the relatives of the hostages who have pointed up the cultural differences -- even the MRTA guerrillas' family members do not fear publicity.
Emma Plasencia, mother of a 16-year-old female rebel, arrived in the site of the hostage crisis on Friday to plead for her daughter to put down her weapons, repent and come out.
"Come back home, we need you," she shouted at one point from a building opposite the besieged residence.
